_comment: qwark's registration, to be merged into settings.json. Not loadable as-is:
settings.json has no comment syntax, so this key is here for a reader and
must not survive into the real file.
TWO THINGS IN THE COMMAND LINE ARE LOAD-BEARING.
1. `|| exit 2` is not belt and braces, it is the only fail-closed exit.
FACT 2026-08-20, confirmed in the Claude Code binary and its docs: exit 0
with no JSON is NO DECISION and the command proceeds, and any non-zero
exit other than 2 is a `non_blocking_error` and the command ALSO
proceeds. Only exit 2 blocks. So a qwark that segfaults, is killed for
running out of memory, or exits 1 the way a Unix program usually reports
failure, lets the command through. qwark recovers from its own panics and
runs in a single goroutine so that it can; this catches everything it
cannot catch itself.
2. The rule paths are given here rather than found, so the policy in force
is readable where the hook is registered rather than implied by which
files happen to be sitting in a directory.
THE RULE FILES MUST NOT BE WRITABLE BY THE USER CLAUDE CODE RUNS AS, nor
may the directory holding them: a writable directory permits
unlink-and-replace, which defeats an unwritable file.
THE DENY LIST IS THE OTHER HALF OF qwark, AND IT IS NOT OPTIONAL.
qwark gates Bash. Write and Edit reach every path below without passing
through it, so a rule qwark enforces against a shell is enforced against
nothing at all unless the same path appears here. Keep this list in step
with the groups in rules/20-paths.toml; they are one control written twice
because two different mechanisms enforce the two halves.
WHY A TASK DEFINITION IS ON THIS LIST. Owner, 2026-08-20: `if they can
write a new file, then they can then get the agent to approve anything`.
`just checks` is a fixed, familiar command line whose meaning lives in a
file in the working tree. Permitting the command permits whatever that file
says tomorrow, and no gate reading command lines can see the difference.
The executors are all denied in rules/10-commands.toml today; if one is ever
permitted, its definition file has to be unwritable or the permission is
worth nothing.
SYNTAX, read out of the Claude Code binary 2.1.233 rather than recalled:
permissions has allow, ask and deny arrays of `Tool(specifier)` strings.
Shipped examples in the binary include "Edit(//etc/*)",
"Edit(~/.claude/settings.json)" and "Bash(rm -rf *)".
`//` is an absolute path, `~/` is home, and a BARE path is relative to
the settings file root -- the project root for project settings and
~/.claude for user settings.
That last point splits this list in two. The absolute and ~ entries
belong in USER settings. The bare task-definition entries are relative
and belong in PROJECT settings, where they resolve against the project
root; putting them in user settings would silently mean ~/.claude/justfile
and match nothing.
SYMLINKS: RESOLVE THESE ON THE MACHINE YOU INSTALL ON. It is unverified
whether Claude Code resolves a symlink before matching, so both spellings
are listed where the target is known. Re-derive with `readlink -f`.
FACT 2026-08-20, measured on the author's machine:
~/.claude/settings.json -> ~/.projects/dotfiles/claude/settings.json
~/.claude/hooks         -> ~/.projects/dotfiles/claude/hooks
~/.zshrc                -> ~/.projects/linux.dotfiles/home/.zshrc
~/bin                   -> ~/.projects/dotfiles/bin
/bin -> /usr/bin and /sbin -> /usr/sbin
~/.bashrc does not exist here.
Those resolved paths are this machine's and are NOT shipped below; add
the ones your machine reports.
